rows.text: Push-triggered metadata updates, reconnection/catch-up and periodic recovery checks, with provider delivery and local reaction latency measured separately.
rows.evidence: docs/validation.md#push-notifications and #subscription-renewal-at-the-real-boundary -- live 2026-09-09: delivery 30.0-32.7 s across eleven samples, local reaction 169-287 ms, measured separately as the box requires. One subscription held 2,999,973 ms, renewed, reconnected, and delivered a fresh change 30,441 ms later. One notification in eleven was never delivered (90 s deadline); the pre-registered interference hypothesis was refuted by an immediately passing retry and the miss stands unexplained; the shipped 30 s poll bounds the impact. Catch-up and periodic recovery are now covered live too (docs/validation.md#catch-up-after-a-reconnection-and-the-periodic-recovery-refresh, benchmarks/live-catchup-and-recovery.json, 2026-09-09): a change made with nothing connected and the poll an hour away was fetched 408 ms after the subscription connected and listed 206 ms later; with no subscription at all the 30 s poll found one in 29,421 ms. Each phase disabled the other and counted zero directory listings before its delta, so neither is explained by activity revalidation. RENEWAL OBSERVED LIVE 2026-09-11: the validator held a real Socket.IO subscription for its full lifetime, Microsoft renewed it, and a change made afterwards was delivered through the renewed connection -- 'Renewed subscription connected; checking a new change through it' followed by a passing delivery. That is a renewal the provider performed rather than one a fixture simulated. STILL OPEN: the one notification in eleven that was never delivered remains unexplained; the periodic figure bounds its impact rather than accounting for it. REPLICATED 2026-09-10 on a separate write-grant validation connection, a different day and build. Catch-up: delta 1536 ms after the subscription connected against 408 ms first time, entry listed 206 ms later -- the same figure to the millisecond. Periodic recovery: delta 29,454 ms against 29,421, a difference of 33 ms across two independent runs. Directory freshness through a real mount: three rounds at 5,147 / 5,297 / 5,103 ms total from change to visible, which is the five-second activity revalidation interval and not push. A mounted view following remote changes: create visible in 2 ms, move in 4,650 ms, delete in 4,450 ms.

NOT ASSERTED BY ANY TEST: the clause 'provider delivery and local reaction latency measured separately'. No unit test can measure a real provider's delivery latency; that clause rests on the live runs recorded in docs/validation.md, and one notification in eleven was never delivered and is still unexplained.

rows.text: Crash/fault tests at every durable transition and concurrent remote edits.
rows.evidence: docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-crash-coverage.json and durable-transition-sites.json for process death: all 31 runtime durable transitions are crossed by a process that then dies, measured rather than read. 2026-09-11, faults below the process: docs/benchmarks/journal-under-io-faults.json. A dm-flakey device switched to error_writes at runtime and back. What was durable before the fault survives it and reads back byte for byte afterwards; new work is refused as JournalError::Storage rather than as corruption -- reporting a refusing device as a corrupt journal would send a user to recovery steps that destroy work the device still holds. A prediction failed usefully: the journal cannot be OPENED on a failing device, because opening opens SQLite and SQLite writes. So its contents are inaccessible during a fault, which is not the same as lost, and the run makes only the second claim. A LYING FSYNC ran the same day: dm-flakey drop_writes acknowledges the write and discards it, and the journal detected it -- sealing was refused as JournalError::Stale, because the journal reads back what it wrote and finds the generation unchanged. Work durable before the lie reads back byte for byte afterwards. The claim is that this injection did not produce wrong-and-confident data, not that no discard can. TORN WRITES were attempted and are inconclusive: corrupt_bio_byte flips a byte in EVERY write bio, so it corrupts ext4's metadata as readily as the journal's data, and the phase hung. A hang in that state is a statement about ext4 meeting corrupted metadata, not about the journal. The targeted version of the same question is already answered -- overwriting a sealed payload makes recovery fail. STILL OPEN: a true power cut cannot be scripted at all. It needs someone at the wall socket or a machine with a controllable PSU, and that clause is why this box is not ticked.
rows.asserted_by: All 31 runtime durable transitions are crossed by a process that then dies, measured rather than read: each site records itself and each crash fixture persists what it reached. 30 are evidenced in a killed child; the preparation recovery in the process that opens the journal afterwards, because that is where recovery runs. See docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-sites.json. a_journal_on_a_failing_device_refuses_without_losing_what_was_durable runs in three phases against one dm-flakey device in CI; re-run with the sealed payload deliberately overwritten, its recover phase fails. Its lie and after_lie phases run in CI on the same device; the tear phases exist but are deliberately not wired in, for the reason recorded in the artifact.

rows.text: Persistent per-file and recursive-folder pinning with storage reservations.
rows.evidence:
TICKED 2026-09-11. Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. COVERED: pins live in the metadata index at schema 7 and survive restart; a reservation is checked against the budget when the pin is made, so a request that will not fit is refused rather than accepted and later evicted; reservations may not claim the whole budget. Reachable from a terminal since 2026-09-10: cirrove pin goes over the control socket to the running daemon, which resolves --path -- including through a shortcut into a linked collection, where a caller outside the daemon recorded the pin under the wrong scope -- and calls materialise_pin or pin_folder. Before that the engine's acting API had no caller outside its own tests and a pin kept nothing. See docs/benchmarks/offline-pinning-reachability.json, which also records the reservation error its own discriminator found: reservations were made in logical bytes while the cache stores a SHA-256 per block, and because pinned blocks are protected the shortfall was never recovered.
MEASURED ON A REAL ACCOUNT 2026-09-11: docs/benchmarks/live-offline-pinning.json. A generated 9,000,000-byte file on the user's business drive, pinned through the same request path the command line uses, reported 9,000,096 bytes resident across three blocks -- the file plus three block digests, which is the reservation correction made the day before arriving at the right answer on a real drive. After the engine was rebuilt and mounted it read back byte for byte with ZERO provider content requests, while an unpinned control in the same folder needed one. The recursive half ran on the same drive the same day: a subtree of two files, walked and pinned through the same request path, reported exactly two files found and complete, reserved 4,000,064 bytes -- the two files plus two block digests -- and both read back through the mount with zero provider content requests. The two-file assertion is the discriminator: a walk that stops after one would keep part of a folder and report success, which is indistinguishable from working until the network is gone.
rows.asserted_by: Persistence: store::pins::tests::a_pin_and_its_protected_blocks_survive_reopening_the_store, and engine::pinning::a_restart_republishes_pins_before_anything_can_evict, which is the stronger of the two because it asserts the ordering rather than only the survival. Recursive folders: engine::pinning::a_folder_pin_covers_every_file_under_it_and_says_what_it_could_not_see and an_unindexed_subtree_is_reported_rather_than_quietly_excluded. Reservations: store::pins::tests::raising_a_pin_counts_only_the_difference_against_the_budget, engine::pinning::a_refused_pin_changes_nothing, content::tests::a_reservation_shrinks_the_budget_the_ordinary_cache_may_fill, and engine::pinning::materialising_a_pin_fetches_its_blocks_and_protects_exactly_those. tests/read_only.rs::a_pin_from_the_command_line_reaches_the_daemon_and_keeps_the_bytes drives a manager, a control socket and the same client function the CLI calls; against the previous source it does not compile. real_a_recursive_pin_keeps_the_files_under_a_folder_readable_offline covers the recursive half through a kernel mount. real_pin_protection_survives_a_restart_and_immediate_cache_pressure covers persistence through Engine::new, a mount and pressure with no pause; two mechanisms establish the protection and either suffices, so it asserts the property rather than which path provides it -- disabling both is what makes it fail. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning is the live check; it is a validator rather than a test, so it asserts on a real account and is not run by CI.

rows.text: Clear unpin/free-space behavior and accurate availability status.
rows.evidence:
TICKED 2026-09-11. Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. COVERED: availability separates what a pin reserved from what it has actually kept, counted from files present in the cache directory rather than from the block index, which is derived state. Unpin is reachable from a terminal and its effect is asserted -- though not the effect first claimed: releasing a reservation raises the ordinary cache budget, so it frees no bytes and correctly leaves the cache as full as it was; what it changes is protection. A refusal reaches the caller with the numbers and the remedy.
2026-09-11: the budget-filling half is built. Engine::pin_budget reports the account's cache allowance, the most pinning may claim of it, what is claimed and what is left, surfaced per account as AccountStatus.pin_budget; PinBudget::explain turns that into a sentence naming both remedies -- unpin something or raise cache_bytes -- and `cirrove pins` prints it under each account's pins, leading with resident against reserved because that is the difference between a pin keeping content and an accounting entry. A caller who can watch the budget fill can act; one who learns about it from a refusal has already been stopped. MEASURED ON A REAL ACCOUNT 2026-09-11, same run: with two pins in force the budget reported 13,000,160 of 234,881,024 pinnable bytes claimed against a 268,435,456-byte cache -- pinnable strictly below the allowance, as reservations may not take the whole of it -- and unpinning returned the full reservation byte for byte. The explanation is a sentence naming what the remainder is for. The live pinning run of 2026-09-11 covers pinning and offline reading, not the budget-filling, cleanup or disk-full behaviour these rows ask about.
rows.asserted_by: engine::pinning::unpinning_releases_the_budget_at_the_cache and store::pins::tests::unpinning_releases_both_the_reservation_and_the_protection cover the free-space half; engine::pinning::availability_separates_what_a_pin_reserved_from_what_it_kept covers the status half. real_unpinned_blocks_stop_being_protected_from_eviction applies the same cache pressure twice, with the pin in force and after it is released, and asserts the blocks survive the first and not the second. real_a_refused_pin_names_the_budget_and_leaves_the_kept_one_alone asserts the refusal names an action, records no pin, disturbs no existing reservation, and leaves the accepted pin readable offline -- the accepted-first assertion is what stops a path that refuses everything from passing. real_the_pin_budget_is_visible_before_it_is_full asserts the figure exists, moves when a pin is made, returns the whole reservation on unpin, and that a full budget names both remedies. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning covers the same clauses live.

rows.text: Offline access and editing of pinned content, including across restart.

TICKED 2026-09-11. Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. COVERED at the durability layer and through the kernel. Reading: a pinned file reads with the provider returning Unavailable and still reads after the engine is rebuilt on the same directory, where the memory cache is empty so the bytes can only come from disk; through a real mount, real_a_pinned_file_reads_offline_through_the_mount_and_an_unpinned_one_does_not asserts the provider read counter did not move and reads an unpinned control that must fail. Editing: a pinned file is edited with the provider unreachable and both the pin and the unsent edit survive a restart of engine and journal -- their views are rebuilt by separate paths that do not consult each other -- and real_a_pinned_file_is_edited_offline_and_both_survive_through_the_mount does the same through a real writable mount.
MEASURED ON A REAL ACCOUNT 2026-09-11: docs/benchmarks/live-offline-pinning.json. A generated 9,000,000-byte file on the user's business drive, pinned through the same request path the command line uses, reported 9,000,096 bytes resident across three blocks -- the file plus three block digests, which is the reservation correction made the day before arriving at the right answer on a real drive. After the engine was rebuilt and mounted it read back byte for byte with ZERO provider content requests, while an unpinned control in the same folder needed one. This covers offline READING. The editing half ran on the same drive the same day: a pinned file edited through a writable mount left a record in the local journal -- the application did not wait for the network to save, which is what the clause is about. A real account cannot be taken offline, so 'offline' here means the read made no provider request and the write asked nothing of it, established by counting rather than by severing the connection. The second is the load-bearing one: the cache's view and the journal's are rebuilt by separate paths that do not consult each other, so surviving together is a claim rather than a consequence. tests/read_only.rs::real_a_pinned_file_reads_offline_through_the_mount_and_an_unpinned_one_does_not covers the reading half through a real FUSE mount, with an unpinned control so a broken offline switch cannot pass it. tests/writable_session.rs::real_a_pinned_file_is_edited_offline_and_both_survive_through_the_mount covers the editing half through a real writable mount; without the pin it fails with EIO on the offline read. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning is the live check; it is a validator rather than a test, so it asserts on a real account and is not run by CI. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning covers reading and editing live.

rows.text: Unsent changes excluded from cache eviction and connection cleanup.
rows.evidence:
TICKED 2026-09-11. Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. COVERED: eviction only ever removes files whose names it recognises as its own block keys plus its own temporaries, so an unsent journal beside the cache is structurally out of reach, and that is asserted rather than argued. The disable half is asserted through a writable mount. Removal now exists: accounts::forget refuses while the account is enabled, refuses while the journal holds unsent records -- naming how many -- and moves the account directory to removed/ rather than deleting it. Building it was necessary before the clause could be tested at all: with no removal path, a test would have asserted that a thing which does not exist does not delete a journal.
MEASURED ON A REAL ACCOUNT 2026-09-11: an unsent journal record is byte-for-byte unchanged after repeated cache reads against a real file on the same account, with the journal sitting beside the cache throughout. Six rounds is pressure rather than saturation and the artifact says so.
rows.asserted_by: content::tests::eviction_never_reaches_outside_its_own_block_names, which places an unsent journal entry beside the cache and a non-block file inside it, drives both deletion passes -- evict and the reconcile that runs on reopening -- and asserts a real block was removed as well, so a pass that deleted nothing could not satisfy it. content::tests::eviction_leaves_a_protected_block_and_takes_the_next_one_instead and the_reconcile_pass_at_mount_time_also_leaves_protected_blocks_alone cover the same two passes for pinned blocks. tests/writable_session.rs::real_unsent_changes_survive_disabling_and_refuse_removal writes through a writable mount with uploads stalled, disables the account and reads the unsent payload back byte for byte, then asserts removal refuses and names what is at stake, leaves the journal where it was, and on an explicit discard moves the data aside rather than deleting it. Without the refusal it removes the account and its one unsent change. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning covers the eviction half live.

rows.text: Disk-full recovery preserves edited data and explains required action.
rows.evidence:
TICKED 2026-09-11. Scope expanded by the user on 2026-09-09. COVERED end to end. Preservation: a refused save leaves the sealed payload and the dirty working copy intact. Explanation: a full local budget and a physically full disk were both JournalError::Quota and both reached an application as ENOSPC, so a user was told 'no space left on device' on a filesystem with gigabytes free while the two remedies are opposite; DeviceFull is now separate and carries its own remedy. A real full ext4 showed that mapping was unreachable, because write_working persists metadata through SQLite before any byte and From<rusqlite::Error> discarded the reason. The daemon reports which of the two it was as AccountStatus.save_refusal. A writable mount now runs on a physically full filesystem, and the without-subject check showed the mapping decides what the KERNEL reports: without it an application gets EIO rather than ENOSPC.
MEASURED ON A REAL ACCOUNT 2026-09-11: the validation account's state, journal and mount on a 160 MB loop-backed ext4 of their own. One save accepted while there was room, then the device filled to its last block, then saves attempted through the kernel: the application got ENOSPC and the daemon recorded kind `device` with a message naming what has to be freed. The provider was reachable throughout, so this is about local storage and not about the cloud being full.
rows.asserted_by: a_genuinely_full_filesystem_explains_what_to_free, which fills the filesystem it is given, asserts ENOSPC outside the journal before trusting any journal error, and fails against the previous code with 'it said: local upload storage is unavailable'. truncate_sparse_writes_and_quota_failures_preserve_the_working_copy and a_full_budget_and_a_full_disk_are_reported_as_different_problems still cover the budget half. real_a_refused_save_is_reported_as_a_budget_and_not_only_as_enospc drives a real mount into its budget through the kernel, asserts ENOSPC still reaches the application, asserts an earlier write was accepted so a wholly broken mount cannot pass it, and fails without the recorder. only_the_two_no_space_refusals_are_recorded_and_they_stay_distinct covers the classification, including that a non-space error leaves the field alone. STILL OPEN: no run has driven a mount on a physically full filesystem, so the device case is evidenced as a mapping and not as a journey. tests/writable_session.rs::real_a_save_on_a_full_device_is_reported_as_a_device_and_not_a_budget covers the device case through a writable kernel mount, with an accepted-before-full save so a mount that refuses everything cannot pass it. CI runs it on the same loop image as its journal-level sibling. validation::pinning::onedrive_pinning covers the device case live when given a filesystem to fill.

rows.text: Personal and business accounts, including multiple simultaneous accounts.
Explicit account, drive and SharePoint library selection.
Linked folders, duplicate links, moved/deleted links and folder-only access.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL, from work on other boxes 2026-09-09 rather than from a check aimed at this one (docs/validation.md#the-same-file-through-two-cold-mounts-with-the-path-off-and-on and #navigating-a-real-collection-while-it-is-being-indexed). The live account is itself an instance of this box: 42 nodes live in its own drive and 183,960 in a linked collection, reached through a single shortcut node whose target names the collection and its root item. Two consequences were measured rather than reasoned about. A fixture that builds its scope from account.drive.id addresses 0.02 percent of what is mounted and fails with 'remote item not found'. An engine given a root id that does not exist inside the named collection serves no listing at all and times out after two minutes without saying why; that now fails immediately with 'root item is not reachable in the named collection'. NOT COVERED: duplicate links, moved or deleted links, and folder-only access, none of which this account exercises.

rows.text: Per-item capabilities, restricted permissions and revoked-access behavior.
Remote creates, edits, moves and deletions update mounted views correctly.
rows.evidence: MOSTLY DONE 2026-09-09 (docs/validation.md#a-mounted-view-following-remote-creates-moves-and-deletions, and #catch-up-after-a-reconnection-and-the-periodic-recovery-refresh). Through a real read-only mount of an isolated account: a remote folder creation became visible in 5,058 ms, a rename in 4,654 ms and a deletion in 4,254 ms, the rename asserted on both halves so that a view adding the new name while keeping the old one fails. All three land at the five-second activity revalidation interval because the fixture watches that directory; a directory nobody is looking at follows the same changes by reconnection catch-up in 408 ms or by the thirty-second poll in 29,421 ms, each measured with the other disabled. NOT COVERED: edits. A content change to an existing file goes through the upload path rather than a namespace mutation, and nothing here exercises it.
rows.asserted_by: validation::remote_changes::onedrive_remote_changes, run live against an isolated account and recorded in docs/validation.md; there is no unit-level assertion, and the box's uncovered clause -- a content edit to an existing file -- has no run at all.

rows.text: Defined filename, package/notebook and unsupported-operation behavior.

Deletion defined end to end: the provider's recycle bin as the default for every file manager without an extension, no local wastebasket created inside the user's drive, permanent deletion reachable only as an explicit second gesture that the window offers too, and both gated on a per-provider capability so a provider without a recycle bin is never presented as recoverable. See [ADR 0008](adr/0008-deletion-and-the-recycle-bin.md).
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-11. One clause of five is closed: the mount root refuses to hold a local wastebasket, in both ways one can appear -- mkdir refuses to create it, rename refuses to fill an existing one. Found as a real directory -- .Trash-1000/ with files/ and info/, created by GNOME Files at 17:57 in a live OneDrive on a writable mount -- not from reading the specification, and confirmed as a remote create in the mutation journal rather than a local shadow. Verified on the live mount after installing the guard: both names refused with EOPNOTSUPP, an ordinary folder still creatable. NOT DONE: the delete prompt still misstates the outcome (GIO reads EOPNOTSUPP as 'no trash' and offers permanent deletion in front of a delete that reaches the recycle bin); permanent deletion has no control verb, no window action and no file-manager extension; the per-provider capability does not exist; an existing wastebasket is not reported to the user. The default already reaches OneDrive's recycle bin via conditional DELETE, but that has never been demonstrated against a live drive by looking in the bin, which is what this box needs an account for.
rows.asserted_by: filesystem::trash::the_names_a_file_manager_would_create_are_refused and ::an_ordinary_folder_that_merely_reads_like_one_is_not for the names; writable_session::real_mount_root_refuses_a_trash_directory_but_a_subdirectory_keeps_the_name and ::real_an_existing_trash_directory_refuses_renames_into_it_but_not_out_of_it for the two refusals through a real kernel FUSE mount, each shown to fail without its guard. Nothing asserts the other four clauses.

rows.text: Documented compatibility matrix backed by real-account checks.
GTK4/libadwaita setup and settings without a terminal in ordinary flows.
Account picker, mount controls, reconnect, connection removal and cleanup.
Tray status and actions using the daemon as the source of truth.
Nautilus badges, pin/unpin actions and consistent status refresh.
Actionable errors, progress, cancellation and conflict resolution.
Keyboard navigation, accessibility, localization and visual verification.

Verify a declared session matrix covering native Wayland and X11, and GNOME and KDE Plasma: windows, dialogs, system dark-style preference and portal-backed folder opening, including cancellation and missing-portal behavior. Record the actual backend and supported session combinations; Xwayland is not native Wayland coverage. Current CI uses Xvfb (X11) only and does not exercise a complete GNOME or Plasma session.

One application identity across the desktop entry, installed application icon, AppStream metainfo, desktop application's D-Bus name and Wayland `app_id`. Verify launcher/window association, including X11, on every declared shell; naming consistency alone is not a runtime check.

Install application-specific scalable and symbolic icons in standard theme locations, replacing the generic application icon. Check dock, launcher and software-centre presentation, including symbolic recoloring.
Implement the tray as StatusNotifierItem over D-Bus. Document the GNOME extension requirement, detect missing tray support and keep all actions available from the window when no tray host is present.

Show recent activity -- remote changes from the delta feed and local saves from the upload journal, with each entry's state -- in the window, and a short form of it in the tray menu. "Recent" means changes to content, not files the user merely opened: a mount stages cache on every read, so a touched-files list would be noise. This is a log and not a level, so it does not ride the coalescing event channel, which by design hands a lagging client current state instead of the entries it missed; it needs its own query. File names appear in the menu and in the window, never in the tray tooltip, which is shown on hover without intent and is visible to anyone looking at the screen or a shared one; the tooltip carries a count. Provide a setting to turn the listing off entirely.

Publish a supported file-manager list beyond the initial Nautilus target, with an explicit Dolphin decision and a shared daemon status contract behind each integration. Unsupported managers must still access mounted files; badge/control availability must be explained.

Preserve actionable, sanitized error causes in the window. Unreadable or invalid settings, an unreachable service and an incompatible service remain distinguishable, with recovery actions and diagnostic detail appropriate to the failure. Never expose credentials or raw provider responses.
Native Arch/AUR, Debian/Ubuntu `.deb` and Fedora `.rpm` packages from the same release, with the clean-system checks in [Distribution](distribution.md).
Signed APT and COPR update channels, release artifacts, source/provenance, supported-version matrix and measured reproducible build procedure.

Fresh installation through sign-in and reboot verified outside development. Validate this on each declared distribution family, including Fedora with SELinux enabled; an Ubuntu CI build is not an installation check.
Upgrade/migration rollback protects settings, credentials and pending work.
Clean uninstall and explicit retention/removal choices for local data.
User documentation, redacted diagnostics and supported-version policy.
Dependency/security review, extended testing and tracked release blockers.

Validate the desktop entry, installed icons and AppStream metainfo in CI, then compare their identity with the running window and application bus name in the supported desktop sessions. Current desktop-file validation alone does not satisfy this gate.

Build and install the daemon and CLI without GTK4/libadwaita present, with separate desktop packaging. The root's default members now exclude the desktop; explicit `--workspace` builds and full contributor checks still include it. A package installation on a clean headless host remains required; headless buildability does not imply unattended browser/keyring setup.
Tagged release and verified installation from the published artifacts.
